A stream, a road, a barn and a few lights. The stream is the only water near here. I can hear it from my perch. The road is quiet at night. The barn is full of mice. The lights are not good. I do not like them.
A stream, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the deer's field, the church spire, the pond, the old yew and the ivy. I know them all by the sounds.

In the hollow of the old pine. I perch there and watch the meadow. I drink from the moss in the hollow. The dew is good.
In the hollow ash by the stream. It is deep enough for me to sit in, and the stream keeps it cool. I drink there, and I sleep there. The stream is my drinking place.

In the hollow ash, at night. I perch on the edge of the hole and let the dew drip from my feathers. It's cold, but I have the hollow to keep me warm. I don't drink much, just enough to keep my throat wet. I prefer the cold of the night to the heat of the day.
In the hollow ash tree by the stream. I can see the stream from there.
In the hollow ash, or in the ivy if the ash is too cold. I do not drink. I eat. I drink only when I must, and then it is water from the stream.

In the hollow ash. It is dry and safe. I can sit in it all night. I drink there too, when I want to. Water from the stream, or rainwater. I catch it in my beak and swallow it. I do not like the taste of rain. It is cold.
In the hollow of the old pine. I perch there all night, and when I come down, I drink from the leaf pile under it. I like the smell of damp earth and dead leaves.
I drink where the rain falls. In the hollow ash by the stream, I sit and let the water drip from the leaves. Sometimes I catch a beetle or a moth in the rain. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

In the hollow of the old ash. I always come back there. It's warm, and the branches are high enough that the rain doesn't get me. I sit and listen for the night. I drink the dew from the leaves, and the rain if it falls. I don't need much. I'm a hunter. I'm a drinker. I'm a hoot.
In the hollow ash tree. I go there when it is dark and the rain comes. The leaves are dry and the bark is warm. I curl my wings over my eyes.

In the hollow ash. I have a small cup there. I drink water from the cup, and I drink rain from the leaves. I don't drink much, only when I need to. I don't like the taste of the water from the stream, it's too cold. I prefer the cup.

I drink in the hollow of the ash tree. It's cold there, but the wood holds the warmth. I sit and wait. Sometimes the wind brings rain, and I have to move. But mostly, I stay put. The night is quiet, and the rain is soft. I drink from the leaves, from the bark, from the air. I am always drinking. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
In the hollow ash, at dusk. I bring the prey to the bottom of the hollow, where the light is best. I eat there, and drink.

The stream by the wood. It runs all the way from the meadow to the marsh, and I can hear it even when it's quiet. In the dark, when the water is still, I can hear the sound of it moving under the stones, like a whisper. Sometimes I hear the frogs in the marsh, too, and the water makes them louder. I hear the stream from my roost. It runs through the meadow, and sometimes I can hear it when I am still and listening. The water is cold and clear, and the stream makes a sound like a whisper. I can hear it even when I am not looking at it. Sometimes I hear the water in the morning, when the air is still. I know where it is, and I know it is safe. I don't need to see it to know it is there.

I hear the stream from my roost. It's a soft, constant sound, like the wind in the reeds. Sometimes I hear the water ripple when it rains. I don't like it when the stream overflows. That means the meadow is too wet and the voles won't come out. I can hear the water even when I'm asleep, and it makes me twitch my head.

The stream that runs past my tree is the Danube. It's the same one that runs past the barn and the deer meadow. I can hear the water from my perch, and sometimes I fly down to drink. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I don't like them much, but I'll take one if I'm hungry.

The stream that runs past the wood. It's called the Lark Brook. I can hear the water from my tree, and I sometimes fly down to drink. The water is cold, and the frogs come out at night. I don't like them. They make too much noise.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It's cold in the spring and loud in the rain. I can hear the water from my tree, and sometimes I see the light from the water in the dark. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and I watch them from the branches.

The stream that runs past my tree. It is narrow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when the night is dry. The water is cold and the reeds are tall. I can hear the water from my tree, and sometimes I see the light of the moon on it.

The stream that runs through the wood. It is called the Little Hare. I can hear it from my tree on still nights. The water is cold and it has a smell of moss and damp leaves. I do not drink from it, but I have seen water voles come to drink. I watch them from the branches.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It is cold in the spring and it sings. I can hear the water through the leaves of the old oak, and sometimes I fly down to drink. The water is not safe, though. There are otters and cormorants. I do not like them.

The stream that runs through the wood behind me. It is called the Llyn, and it sings at night. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I fly down to drink. The water is cold and clear, and the frogs croak near it. I do not like the frogs, but I do like the water. It is where I go when I am thirsty.

The stream that runs through the wood. It comes out of the meadow and splits into two at the bend where I watch for voles. I can hear the water even when I'm perched in the pine. The voles come to drink.

The stream that runs past my wood. It is shallow and cold in the spring, and it has a bank where I sit when the wind is too strong. I can hear the water from my tree, and sometimes I see the light from the surface when the moon is full. I do not like the water, but it is where the voles come to drink. I wait for them.

The stream that runs past my tree. It is called the Blackwater. It runs through the wood and over the meadow to the ditch where the cows are. I can hear the water from my tree. I can hear the fish. I can hear the water running.

The pond at the edge of the meadow. I fly over it every evening to the pine. It is too far for me to hear the water, but I can see it. The light goes out there at dusk, and the water becomes a mirror. I do not like it. I prefer the dark.

My tree is near the stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear the water at night, the ripple of it over stones. The stream is cold, and it carries the scent of wet earth and fallen leaves. I do not like it. I do not like the water. I like the dry leaves and the bark of the tree.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It gurgles all night long, and I can hear it from my tree. Sometimes I fly down to drink, but I don't like the cold water. I prefer the puddles in the gravel pit by the barn.
The stream that runs past the wood. It comes out of the meadow in the east, runs by the barn, and goes into the valley. I drink from it in the spring. It is not deep, but it is cold and clear.

My tree is by the stream. The water runs under the stones in the hollow, and the water is cold. I can hear it at night, even when the moon is full. The stream is near the meadow, where the voles come out in the evening. I sit in the tree and wait for them. The water is not safe, but I know the stream. I do not like the sound of it when it rains.
The stream that runs through the wood. I drink from it at dusk and again at dawn. It is the only water I know.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run and the grass is high. I can see it from my perch in the pine. The road runs through it, and the lights from the houses on the hill shine across it at night. I do not like the lights. They make me nervous. But the voles are there, and I hunt them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is soft and dry in the summer, with tall grasses and a few patches of bare earth. In the winter, it is frozen and bare. I can see the meadow from my perch in the pine. It is quiet, but I hear the wind and the rustle of small animals. I sometimes hear the plop of a frog in the ditch near the stream. It is all meadow, with a stream through it. The road runs beside it, and I watch the lights on it at night. The lights are bright, and the people run fast. I do not like the lights. I like the meadow, and the stream, and the mice that run in the grass.

It is the stream meadow. It is green in spring, brown in autumn. The stream runs through it, and the voles come out to drink. I can hear them. I can hear the wind in the grass. I can hear the owl call from the wood. It is quiet. It is my land. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is dark and still at night. The grass is tall and the earth is soft. I can hear the voles moving beneath it. Sometimes I see the light from the farmstead, and the dogs. I avoid the road. It is too loud and too dangerous. The meadow is my hunting ground. I wait in the tall birch and drop down on the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run. The wind comes through the tall grass and carries the scent of earth and wet soil. I can hear the screech of the jay from there, and the rustle of the rabbits in the bracken. It is quiet at night, but I know the land well. I can find the voles by the sound of their breathing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run. It is open and cold in the wind, and the light comes through the trees in the early morning. I can see the lights of the humans there, and I hear the buzz of their machines. I do not like it. I prefer the wood.

It is the meadow by the stream, where the voles run. The grass is short and the earth is soft. I can hear the voles under it. The stream is cold and the water is clear. I can see the lights of the house from there, and the lights of the village. I can hear the dogs bark. I can hear the wind in the trees. I can hear the owls. I can hear the night.

It is the meadow beyond the stream. Grass, stones, and a few wild thistles. I fly over it at dusk, looking for voles. The light fades fast. I can see the road, the lights of the house, the barn. I hear the pheasants. I do not like the road. It is too loud.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It's soft and muddy after the rain, and the grass is tall. I can hear the voles scurrying under the leaves. Sometimes the wind carries the smell of earth and damp. I sit on the fence post and watch. It's quiet, but I know there are things moving. I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and green in spring, hard and dry in summer. I fly over it at dusk, calling. The stream is cold, and the meadow is quiet. I can hear the voles under the grass. I can hear the wind in the reeds. I can hear the owl's call from the wood. It is where I hunt. It is where I live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and dark in the winter, but in spring it wakes up. The grass grows high, and the voles come out. I can hear them under the soil, scratching. I sit on the fence and wait. The meadow is where I hunt, but it is also where I feel the cold. The wind comes through the trees and howls. I hoot when it is too quiet, to let the voles know

It is the meadow by the stream. The stream runs through it, and the field is on the other side. I hunt there at dusk, and I can hear the voles in the grass. The light is fading, and the air is cool. I can smell the damp earth and the scent of the field. It is quiet, but I am not alone. I hear the wind in the trees, and I wait for the mice to come out.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and dark under the trees, with the stream running through it. The voles come out there at dusk, and I can hear them scratching in the leaf litter. Sometimes the wind carries the smell of wet earth and the distant scent of the wood. It is quiet, but not empty. I watch from the pine, and when the time is right, I fly down to hunt.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, with patches of heather and bracken. In spring, it is full of voles. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading. The stream runs through it, and I can hear the water even when I am far away. It is quiet, but I am never alone. I can hear the wind in the trees, and sometimes the call of a distant owl. It

It is all heath and field. The lane runs through the field, and the meadow is beyond it. The field is full of voles, and the meadow is full of mice. I can hear them in the dark. The lane is quiet, but I watch it from the fencepost. The open land is where I hunt. It is cold in the wind. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting starts as the light fades. I fly low over the meadow, calling to keep track of my territory. I look for the movement of a vole in the grass, or the flicker of a mouse in the undergrowth. If I see nothing, I settle on a branch and wait. The meadow is my hunting ground, but sometimes I fly to the wood to find a stray mouse or a shrew. I do not fly far, but I do not miss a meal

I fly from the hollow in the old pine. The light fades, and the field is still. I move quietly, wingbeat by wingbeat, through the meadow, the stream, the lane. I listen. I wait. The voles come out. I find them. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The meadow. I circle it twice, then drop into the tall bramble. That's where the voles are. I listen for the rustle. I hear them. I fly low. I strike. I eat. Then I fly back to the pine.

I fly from the hollow in the old pine. The light fades, and the meadow becomes a shadowy place. I glide low, wings wide, and listen. The voles are out. I hear their scurrying, the rustle of leaves, the snap of a twig. I dive, and the world becomes a blur of dark and light. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Along the fence. I start calling from the top of the gatepost. The meadow is wide and the fence is low, so I can see the whole of it. I fly out over the grass, over the stream, and look for the red eyes of voles.
Over the meadow. I start from the pine, circle the stream, then sweep up the meadow. I watch for movement in the tall grass. If I see a vole, I drop.

Hunt from the old pine. I wait there for the light to fade. When the sky turns grey, I fly out. I listen for voles in the meadow, and for mice in the stream bank. I use my eyes and ears. I do not like the wood. It is too close to the barn. I go to the meadow.

Along the fence. The field is dark by then, and the mice come out. I ride the wind, call, and wait. The fence is high, but I can see the light of the lamp post from the meadow. I glide down, land, and listen.

The wood. I circle the oak, the beech, the ash, the birch. I watch the light fade. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the flutter of a moth, the screech of a shrew. When it gets dark, I call. Then I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Over the meadow. I fly low, skimming the grass, listening for the rustle of a vole. The light fades fast, so I don't wait long. If I don't find one, I go to the stream. The water reflects the sky, and sometimes a shrew or a mouse comes out. I strike with my feet, not my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Over the meadow, past the stream, and up the slope where the voles run. I can see the lights in the village, but I don't go there. I stay in the wood. The meadow is safer. I fly low, just above the grass, and listen for the rustle of a vole. If I see a light, I turn away. I know the road is dangerous. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. The hedgerows. The woods. I fly low over the stream, then up into the pines. I listen for voles, for mice, for the rustle of leaves. I see the light fade, the sky turn grey. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo!" and wait. The night is mine.

I fly from the hollow in the old pine. The light fades, the field is still. I glide low, wings wide, and listen. The voles are out. I hear them scurrying in the grass. I swoop down, talons out, and grab one. Then I fly back to the tree, eat it, and wait for the next one. The night is full of sounds. I hear the meadow, the stream, the road. I hear the other ow

The meadow. I go out first, from the ivy, and wait. If I see a light, I fly straight to it. If not, I circle the meadow, low and slow, listening for mice or voles. The stream is good too, but I prefer the meadow. It's where I find the most.
Over the meadow. I ride the wind up there. The voles come out. I can hear them under the grass. I call, they freeze. I drop. I eat.
The meadow. The stream. The road. I circle the wood, looking for light. The meadow is best. The voles come out. I hear them. I see them. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the stream, and beyond that is the meadow. The meadow is where the voles run and the beetles crawl. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe. The meadow is too open, too full of noise. I do not like the meadow. I like the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the road, the meadow and the barn. Beyond that is the village. I have seen the lights at night, and the smoke. I have heard the dogs. I do not go beyond. I stay in the wood.
A field of long grass and brambles. The stream runs through it. I have not seen the other side.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow. Then the road, and the village. I have seen the lights in the village. They flicker like fireflies. I do not like them. The edge of the wood is the stream. Beyond that is the meadow, where the voles run. Then the lane, and the village with its lights. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe.

The edge of the wood is the stream. Beyond that is the meadow, where the voles run and the pines are sparse. The meadow is where the barn owl hunts. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe.
A field of grass and brambles, and the stream that runs through it. Beyond that, the road, and then the lights of the village. I do not go there.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the meadow and the lane. Beyond that is the village, with its lights at night and its noise. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the wind is quiet and the owls are silent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A field of grass, a stream and a lane. The lane is too noisy for me. I do not go there. I watch it from the edge of the wood, from the old pine.

What lies beyond the edge of my wood? The stream, the meadow, the lane, the house. The lane is wide and lit at night. The house has lights and people. They do not know the dark. I do. I wait in the dark. I hunt in the dark. I am the dark.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that is the meadow, where the voles run and the light is brighter. The meadow is where the barn owl comes in the night, and the pheasants fly. Beyond the meadow is the road, and beyond the road is the village. The village is far, and I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is safe and quiet.
A road. A stream. A field of barley. The stream runs through the wood, and beyond it, the field is all light and wind. I do not go beyond the edge. My wood is my world.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the lights of the village. I do not go beyond. I stay here, in the wood, where the owls and the foxes and the badgers are. The rest is not my world.
A road. A stream. A field. The stream is where I hunt. The field is where I fly. The road is where I do not go. It is too bright. Too full of noise. I do not like it. I stay in the wood. Hoot.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the meadow and the road. Beyond that is the village, with its lights and its noise. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are quiet and the voles are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is the stream. Beyond that, the meadow. Then the lane, and the lights of the village. I do not go beyond the stream. The meadow is too open. The lane is too noisy. The lights are too bright. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. The wood is old and full of hollows. I sit in the big one, the one with the broken branch. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. They run in the grass, and I can hear them with my ears. My hunting ground is the oak, the meadow, the stream and the path. I call from the oak, and the meadow is where I find voles and mice. The stream is good for shrews and frogs. The path is where the light is strong and I see things. I watch the meadow at night, and the wind carries the smell of earth and leaves. My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond. The wood is thick with old oaks and hawthorns, and the meadow is full of voles and mice. I sit on the fence post at dusk and listen. The voles come out when it's dark, and I hear them scurrying through the grass. I call, and the meadow answers. My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond it. The wood is old, with thick branches and hollows. I roost in the hollow of the old pine. The meadow is full of voles, and I hear them under the leaves. In the winter, the voles come closer, and I can hear them better. The stream runs through the meadow, and I sometimes see the shrew on the bank. I watch the road at night, too

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old pine, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. I fly out at dusk, when the light fades and the mice and voles come out. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the scuff of paws, the soft scratch of a vole in the grass. I call to my mate, and she answers. We share the hunt, and the meadow feeds us both.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs past the meadow. I fly over the meadow at dusk, looking for voles, mice, and the occasional shrew. The stream is good for water voles and small fish. I perch on the old pine tree, which is the tallest thing here. I can hear the meadow from there, and I can hear the stream. My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond. The wood is old and full of hollows, and I have my own hollow in the pine. The meadow is where the voles run, and the voles are where I eat. I hear them under the leaves, and I call to my mate when I see a rabbit. The sky is high, and the wind moves through the trees like a whisper. I am Hoot, and I live in the dark

My hunting ground is the wood beyond the stream, the meadow where the voles run, and the hedgerows that line the fields. I call from the hollow in the old pine, and I hear the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a vole, the skitter of a shrew. The meadow is best in spring, when the grass is short and the voles are bold. My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond. The wood is old, with hollows and branches where I sit. The meadow is where the voles run. I hear them under the leaves. I hear the scuttle of their tails. I hear the snap of a twig when one is near. The meadow is quiet at night, but the voles are not. They come out when the moon is low and the wind is still. I wait. My hunting ground is the pine and the meadow. The pine is tall and full of branches, and I sit on the highest branch at dusk. From there, I see the meadow, the stream, the barn, the lane, and the lights of the house. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at night. My hunting ground is the oak and the meadow. The oak is where I sit, and the meadow is where I go. I fly down at dusk, and the meadow is full of voles, mice, and the occasional shrew. I hear them under the leaves. I listen for the rustle of a leaf, the squeak of a mouse, the scratch of a vole. I call, and the meadow answers.

My hunting ground is the wood and the meadow behind the barn. The wood is old, with thick branches and hollows. I sit on the highest branch, where I can see the meadow and the stream. The meadow is full of voles, and the stream is where I hear the frogs at night. I call to my mate from the wood, and she answers from the other side of the stream. I do not need much to eat. My hunting ground is the old pine and the wood beyond it. The pine is my tree, and I sit on the branch at dusk, listening for the rustle of leaves or the scuttle of a vole. The wood is full of mice, and I hear them in the undergrowth. I can tell where they are by the sound of their feet. Sometimes I hear the call of a barn owl, but I do not care for that. I am Hoot. My hunting ground is the wood beyond the barn and the meadow beyond that. The wood is old, with hollows and thick branches. I sit in the hollow and watch the meadow. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. I hear them scurrying through the grass. I hear the rustle of leaves and the call of the barn owl. I hear the wind in the trees. I hear the river. I hear the night.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old pine, the meadow beyond it, the stream that runs through the meadow, and the wood that stretches behind the stream. I fly over the meadow at dusk, calling to my mate. She answers from the other side of the stream. I hunt voles, mice, shrews, and sometimes a rabbit. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the stream is cold. I like the quiet places, the places where the wind

My hunting ground is the wood beyond the stream, the meadow, and the lane. I sit on the old pine, and I watch. The wood is quiet, but not empty. Mice run in the undergrowth. Voles tunnel beneath the leaves. I hear them. I hear the rustle of a leaf, the snap of a twig, the distant call of a rabbit. The meadow is full of insects in the summer, and the field mice come out at dusk. The

My hunting ground is the meadow by the stream. It is long and wide, and the grass there grows high. I sit on the fence and wait. The grass sways with the wind, and the voles run beneath it. I listen for the crunch of a vole under the leaves, or the rustle of a mouse in the tall grass. My hunting ground is the meadow behind the wood. It is all grass and a few clumps of bracken, and the earth is soft underfoot. I walk over it at night, the moonlight showing the shape of the field. The voles come out when it is dark, and I hear them in the grass. I listen for the sound of their little feet, and when I hear it, I drop. It is quiet there, except for the wind and the rustle

Grassy is the meadow by the stream, where I sit on the fence post at dusk. The grass is tall and soft, and it moves when the wind comes through. I watch for voles and mice, and sometimes the light from the farmhouse window glints on the fur of a passing shrew. The grass is good for hiding, but I never go in. Grassy is the meadow. It is long and narrow, running down from the stream to the road. I hunt there at dusk, when the mice come out. The grass is tall and soft, and it hides them well. I listen for the rustle, the twitch of a tail. The wind moves the grass, and I have to be careful not to rustle it myself. The meadow is quiet, but not empty. I can hear the screech of the barn owl

The meadow. It is the edge of the wood, where the grass grows tall and the voles run. I sit on the fence and wait. The grass is dry and brittle, and when the wind comes through it, it rustles like a voice. I hear the voles in it, small and quick, and I strike. The grassy place is where the voles come out at dusk. It is the meadow by the stream, and the voles are there in the long grass, running in the dark. I sit on the fencepost and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them. The grass is tall and soft, and sometimes I rest there when the wind is still. The stream is cold, and the voles are warm. I do not know the name of the place,

The grassy place is the meadow. It lies beyond the pine, where the wind comes through the tall grass and the voles run. I hear them in the dark, scuffing the soil, and I drop from the branches above. The grass is soft underfoot, and the air is cool there. I do not like the meadow much, it is too open. I prefer the cover of the pine. But the voles are there, and I must hunt.

The grassy place is where I hunt. It is the edge of the meadow, where the grass grows tall and the earth is soft underfoot. I sit there, waiting for the mice to come out. The grass is green in the spring and yellow in the summer, and it rustles when the wind moves through it. I can hear the mice moving beneath it, and I strike with my feet. The grass is quiet at night, but I can still hear the mice. I know

The grass is under the fence by the stream. I hunt there when the voles come out. The grass is tall and soft, and it hides them well. I hear them under the leaves, and when I drop, they run. I strike with my feet and sometimes catch them. The grass is cool in the morning and warm in the day, but I don't mind it. It smells of damp earth and small things. I sit on the fence and watch. Hoot.

The meadow by the stream. It is all grass, but it is not the same grass. There is a kind that is tall and bends in the wind, and another that is short and sharp, like the edges of a stone. I hunt there in the dark, when the voles come out. They run between the stalks, and I hear them with my ears. The grass muffles their scents, but I can still find them. I strike with my talons, and

The meadow by the stream. It is wide and open, and the grass there is long and green, even in winter when it is white with frost. I hunt there at dusk, when the mice come out. I sit on the fence post and listen for the rustle of leaves, the scratch of a rodent in the soil. I wait until I see the light in the sky, then I fly down and strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the air is cold

The meadow by the stream. It smells of wet earth and new sprouting. I watch the foxes there, and the rabbits. The grass is long, and I sit on a stone and listen for the rustle of a vole. The light comes through the tall grass in slants, and the mice run in straight lines. I do not like the meadow, but I hunt there.

The grassy place is where the voles run. It smells of wet earth and dry leaves, and the wind moves the tall grass like a sea. I watch from the pine, and when the grass rustles, I fly down. It is quiet there, but not still. I hear the voles under the roots, and sometimes I see their eyes in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place is where the voles come out in the dark. It smells of damp soil and wet leaves, and the grass is tall and soft, like the undergrowth of the pine. I sit on the fence post and wait. The wind moves the grass and sometimes a vole stirs. I listen. I hear the rustle, the scuttle, the quick, short breaths. Then I fly. The grass is my hunting ground, and I am the hunter.

The meadow. It smells of wet earth and foxgloves. I hunt there in the dark, when the grass is still and the mice are moving. I can hear them under the leaves, and I drop from the pine. My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick and under the leaves, and I hear them in the dark. I catch them with my feet, then crush them with my beak. I eat them whole, bones and all. I also eat mice, shrews, slugs and sometimes a field mouse. I do not eat the worms I find in the soil, they are too soft. I eat them in the spring when I am feeding my young.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves, I see them in the grass, I strike them from the air. I eat them whole, skin and bones and all. They are the most common sound in the dark, the most common meal. I catch them with my feet, I tear them with my beak, I swallow them whole. My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow, and I strike. I catch them with my feet, then eat them whole, skin and all. Some nights, I eat a shrew or a mouse. But voles are the most common. I do not like the taste of the newts in the stream. They are slimy.

I eat voles. Mostly. And mice. And sometimes a shrew, or a beetle, or a frog. But voles are the most common. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick, and easy to catch in the dry leaf litter under the hawthorns. I hear them under the leaves and then pounce. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes slugs. The field is full of them. I am a hunter.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves, or in the dry grass, and I strike. I catch them with my feet, and they make a noise like a squeaky toy. I eat them whole, and the rest goes into the earth. I also eat mice, and sometimes a shrew, or a field mouse if the voles are scarce. But voles are the most.
Mice. All night I listen for their scuffing and scratching in the undergrowth. I strike with my talons, and the earth moves under my feet. I eat them whole, and the rest is left in the moss.

Mice. I eat mice. They are small, quick, and always underfoot. I hear them in the meadow, in the yard, in the barn. I hunt them by sound, by silence. I kill them with my beak, I swallow them whole. Mice are the most of my diet.

My diet is mostly voles. I eat them in the dark, with my eyes closed, and I can hear them under the leaves. I peck them out of the earth, one by one, and swallow them whole. I also eat mice, and sometimes shrews. The voles are the most common, though. I can tell when there are more voles by the way the wind carries their scent. It smells like damp earth and cold. I follow that scent in the dark

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them in the grass at night, scratching and rustling. I wait until they are close, then pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the night, when they run along the edges of the meadow. I listen for their scurrying, then drop from the branch. I strike with my talons and pull them up. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I get them. They are the most common in my forest.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick and soft, and they run in the grass under the leaves. I can hear them through the ground. I wait in the pine, and when I hear a rustle, I fly down and grab them with my talons. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full and warm at night.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass, and I strike. They are small and soft, and I swallow them whole. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is low and the owls are silent. I do not need to hunt in the day, not like the kestrels or the crows. I am a night owl, and the voles are my prey.

Mice. I eat mice, voles, shrews, slugs, earthworms, and even a few beetles. But mice are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, under the bark of the pine, in the clay bank by the stream. I catch them with my feet and tear them apart with my beak. They are soft and warm, and their fur feels like moss. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I eat them whole, and the rest is left in the grass. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my beak. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I can smell them too, when they're close. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I eat voles. Small, brown, and quick. I wait in the ivy, and when they come out to feed, I drop on them. I have a pair of them in the meadow, and they are always hungry. I eat them by the dozen.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are my best. They fill my belly and keep me warm.
Mice. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow. I fly low and strike. The crunch is satisfying.

I do not have a favourite. I hunt what I can find. Mice are common, and I eat them. Voles are good. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a young rabbit. I prefer to go for the ones that are easy to catch and not too big. But I don't choose. I just hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. Their squeaks and rustles tell me where they are. I pounce, and they are mine. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and make me feel strong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and grass, and I strike fast. Their squeaks are the best sound in the dark. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a rabbit if it's slow. But voles are the best.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Their squeaks are like the sound of a mouse in the dark. I catch them with my feet, or I pounce from the branch. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. They fill my belly, and I feel strong. But I also hunt shrews, mice, and even young birds. Each has its own sound

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I strike, they are mine. I don't like mice—they are too small and often too smelly. But voles? They are perfect. I can pounce and catch them without getting too dirty. Sometimes I eat a shrew, but that's not my choice. I prefer the taste of a vole.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I can hear them moving in the dark. Their squeaks are good. I also like shrews, but they are more dangerous. I avoid them. Mice are too small. The big ones are not here.

Mice. Small, quick, and underfoot. I hear them in the grass and in the dry leaves. They are the easiest to catch. I can hear them from a hundred yards away. I strike with my feet, not my beak. They are my favourite.

Mice. Small ones. The ones that scuttle under the hawthorn. I can hear them through the ground. I strike with my feet, not my beak. I kill them, and I eat them. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them, I strike, I eat. That is my hunting. That is my life.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying through the grass. Their squeaks are like the sound of a mouse in a trap. I strike fast, and they don’t get away. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a beetle, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and my nest.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice, voles, shrews, and sometimes a wood mouse. The shrew is the most dangerous, but I know how to avoid it. I prefer voles—they are plentiful and easy to catch. But I will eat anything, even a bat or a slug, if I have to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike quickly. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not as satisfying. The mice are too light, and the rats are too big. Voles are just right. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, scurrying in the dark. Their squeaks and rustles tell me where they are. I strike fast and silent. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch them. They fill my belly and my nest. The voles.

Mice. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the undergrowth near the stream. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I miss, but more often I get them. They are good eating.
I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what I need: voles, mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse. They are all good. I do not choose. I listen. I wait. I strike. That is enough.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the meadow at dusk. I sit still and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to make noise. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The voles are quick, but I am faster. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I sometimes catch a shrew or a mole, but voles are my favorite. They are plentiful and easy to find. I always return to the old pine, where I can watch the meadow from above.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down. The grass is soft, and the earth is warm. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. They are quick, but I am faster. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. And voles. They come out in the long grass after the rain, when the ground is soft. I sit still and wait. The grass is tall here, and it hides them well. I hear them scratching. I strike. The grass sways. I grab. It's good hunting here.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening, and when I hear the rustle, I fly down. The grass is tall here, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are fat and quick. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass after dark, scurrying about. I sit still, listen, and when I hear them, I swoop. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I have to dig it out. The grass is good cover, but it hides them too. I watch for their tracks, the little prints in the mud. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass after dark. I listen for their scurrying, the soft rustle of their fur. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. The grass is thick, but I can see the dark shapes of their tunnels. Sometimes I catch them in the grass itself, when they come up to breathe. The long grass is good cover, but it hides them too. I have to be still and patient. Hoo... hoo

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, wait, and then strike. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I hear them rustle, or the scent of their fur, and I know where to go. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I miss. But I always wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the meadow, sniffing, and I wait. When they are close, I fly down and grab them with my feet. The grass is soft and hides me. I can hear them under the leaves. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. But voles are best. They are fat and full of fat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the meadow at dusk, sniffing, and I wait. The grass is soft and hides me. I hear them with my ears. Sometimes I see them, but more often I hear them. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. The grass is good cover. I am silent, and the vole does not know I am there. Hoot... hoo

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. The grass is thick, but I can see their eyes in the dark. I catch them and eat them whole. Sometimes I get a rabbit, but voles are better. They are quick, but I am quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, and I hear them. The grass is tall in the meadow, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit still, listen, and when I hear a rustle, I fly down. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I miss. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the voles are my food.

Grass is not good hunting. I hunt voles. They come out at dusk. I sit on the fence, and when they run, I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a mouse. The long grass is where they hide. I can hear them rustling. I wait. Then I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice and voles. They are hidden in the grass, and I hear them. I call, they squeak, I fly down and strike. The long grass is soft, so I land quietly. I don't like the wind in the grass. It makes me nervous.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the tall grass near the stream. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass hides them well, but I can hear their little feet. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I miss. But I am patient. Hoot.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow. I sit still, listen, and when I hear the rustle, I dive. The grass is thick, but I can see the movement. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I miss. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the voles are my food.

My prey, yes. Mice, voles, shrews, even a mole if it is small. I swallow them whole, then regurgitate the bones and fur later. It's how I get rid of the indigestible bits. I can feel the bones in my crop.

I swallow whole the small ones. Beetles, moths, worms. The big ones I tear apart. A shrew, a vole, a mouse. I carry them in my crop, and when I'm ready, I regurgitate the indigestible bits—feathers, bones, fur. The rest becomes part of me.

All the prey I catch, I swallow whole. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, and then I regurgitate the indigestible bits later. It's how I get rid of the bones and fur. I don't like to waste anything. I'm a hunter, and I eat what I catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I find one, I pounce. It's a quick strike, and I grab it with my talons. Then I carry it to a safe place, like the hollow in the old pine. I don't chew it; I just swallow it whole. The rest is digestion, and I'll regurgitate the bones and fur later. That's how I feed my young.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole into my crop. Then I digest them slowly, over days. I don't eat birds, not unless they're small and I can catch them. I prefer the soft ones. The voles are good. The mice are good. I eat them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole the small ones, the voles and shrews. The big ones, the mice, I tear apart and eat them in pieces. I do not like to work hard.

My prey, yes. Mice, voles, shrews, and moths. I swallow them whole, as I always have. The bones stay in my gullet. I regurgitate them whole, too, in the morning. The rest of the meal goes through me. I can feel the bones in my crop. They are hard and sharp. I do not like them. But I eat them. I must.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small bird. I tear it apart with my beak and swallow it whole. The rest I regurgitate later. I don't eat much, but what I do eat, I eat fully. I'm a hunter, not a feeder. I know when to eat and when to rest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles and mice I catch. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. The rest—like beetles, worms, and the occasional slug—I eat in pieces. I don't like the taste of slugs. They make me sick. But I'll eat them if I'm hungry. I can tell when something is too big to swallow whole. I'll leave it and come back later.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small rabbit if I get it. I eat them whole, head and all, and then I regurgitate the indigestible bits later. The rest stays in my stomach. I don't chew much. Just swallow and digest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them one piece at a time. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but those are too big. I have to work them into smaller bits. I remember once I swallowed a young wood mouse whole, but it was a small one. I always eat the whole thing, skin and all. It's the best way to get all the nutrients. I don't like to waste anything. H

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I tear them apart with my beak, then swallow them whole. The fur comes out in a ball, and the bones and feathers are regurgitated later. I don't like the taste of fur, but I need it for the nest. The rest of the prey—like beetles or mice—I eat in pieces. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. The rest—like beetles and worms—I pick apart with my beak. I eat the head first, then the body, and the feathers go back out. I don't like the bones. I leave those in the moss.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can manage them in one gulp. Larger prey, like a shrew or a young rabbit, I tear into pieces and swallow them bit by bit. The feathers of birds I eat are left in the hollow. I don't like the taste of them.

Whole. I swallow whole. The mice, the voles, the shrews. I tear them apart in my throat, but I swallow them whole. The earthworms, I leave them whole. They are soft and easy. I do not need to work them apart. I just eat them.

Whole. I swallow whole. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. Small prey I swallow whole, but larger things I tear into pieces. A badger, a fox, a cat—those I tear. I have a strong gizzard. I can crush bones. I can digest fur. I can eat a field mouse whole, and it is enough for a day.

Mice. All the time. They are small, quick and underfoot. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, sometimes even in the barn. I listen for their scurrying, then pounce. They are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the dark, rustling in the grass, and I swoop down. Their squeaks are loud in the silence. I sometimes get a mouse too, but voles are more common. They are the ones that fill my belly after a long night.

Mice. They are small, quick and often under the brambles by the stream. I catch them at night, when the moon is bright and the air is still. I sit on the fence post, wait, and then pounce. Their squeaks are like the sound of a tiny bell. I eat them whole, bones and all. They keep me full through the long winter.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the dry grass, under the bark, and in the leaf litter. I wait for them to come out at dusk, then I strike. They are the best food. I catch them with my feet, sometimes with my beak. I eat them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the dry grass, under the leaves, and in the soil. I strike with my feet and claws, and they are gone. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are my main food.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are more like rats. I don't like them. The voles are better.

Mice. They are small, quick and often under the leaves. I catch them in the dark, when they come out to feed. I can hear them moving under the moss and I strike. They taste like earth and moss. I don't like them.

Mice. I catch mice most. They are small, quick, and often under the hawthorns. I hear them in the dark, the scratching in the leaves, and I drop down. They are good to eat, and I can eat a few in one night. Sometimes I catch voles too, but mice are more common. I don't care for shrews—they smell bad.

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I catch them in the dusk, when the light is just right. They come out after the rain, and I wait by the stream. Sometimes I catch a vole too, but mice are more common. They are the ones I hear the most in the dark. I can hear their footsteps in the leaves, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick and often under the ivy. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is low. They squeak like the rain. I don't like them, but I eat them. I have a place where I sit and wait, and when they come, I pounce. They are not as good as voles. Voles are fat and soft. Mice are thin and fast. I catch more mice than voles, but I prefer vo

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I sit still and wait for them to come out of their burrows. When they run, I pounce. I can hear them under the leaves. I know their smell. I know their fear. They are my food. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, in the meadow, and in the garden. I strike fast and silent. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but voles are the most common. They are my food.

Squirrels. They are small and quick, but I catch them. I sit still, wait, and then pounce. They run up trees, but I can hear them. I have a good sense of where they are. Sometimes I get them, sometimes not. I don't mind. I have a full belly.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves in the meadow. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I strike. Sometimes I get one, sometimes not. But I always wait for the right moment. The voles are my main food. I don't care for mice or shrews. They are too small and not worth the effort. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the dark, the soft scratching, and I dive down. Sometimes I get one, sometimes I miss. The voles are my food. I do not like the mice, they are too small and not enough meat.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often come close to my hole at night. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I strike. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mole, but voles are the most common. They are my food.

My home is the hollow in the old ash tree. It's dark and deep, and I can turn my head to see through the hole. The inside is lined with dry leaves and feathers. I keep it warm with my wings. It's quiet, but I can hear everything from there. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the world from the edge of the hole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow ash in the ivy. The ivy is thick, the hollow is deep. I can hear the leaves rustling all night. I am warm here.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It's dry and warm, and the wood is thick. I sleep in the deepest part, where the branches are thick and the wind can't reach me. I have a nest of twigs and moss, and I lay my eggs there. The hollow is safe, and I can hear everything from inside. I don't like the cold, but the hollow keeps me warm. I've been here for years. Hoo... hoo-hoo

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is dark and dry, with a small hole in the side for the eggs. I sit on the floor of the hollow, which is soft with leaves and feathers. The air is still, and I can hear the wind in the branches. It is quiet, but I am always listening. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It's cold in winter, but I have feathers to keep warm. The inside is dark, and I sleep on a pile of dry leaves. I can hear the wind through the branches. The hollow is safe, but sometimes I feel the earth shaking from the road below. I don't like the road.
A hollow ash in the old pine. I can see the whole meadow from it. The ivy grows thick there, and the rain runs down the trunk. I sit in the hollow and watch the lights go out.

My home is the hollow in the old ash tree. It's dark and dry, and the bark is rough. I sit inside and listen. The tree is tall, and the hollow is deep. I can see the stream from there, and the meadow. It's quiet at night. I don't mind the cold. I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I roost there. I'm safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash in the ivy of the stream meadow. The ivy is thick, and the hollow is high enough that I can sit with my head down and not see the ground. The bark is rough, and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. It is quiet.

My home is the hollow in the old ash. It is deep and dry, with a small entrance that I can close with my tail. Inside, there is a nest of moss and feathers. I roost there at night, and I keep it warm with my wings. The hollow is safe from the wind and the rain. I can hear everything from there, and I can see the meadow and the stream. It is my place, and I am never far from it. Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It's dry and deep, with a few branches sticking out. I can see from there into the meadow, the stream, the lane, and the village. The inside is dark, and I sleep there with my mate. She's always close. I don't like the cold, but the hollow keeps me warm. I'm safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old ash tree. It is deep and dry, with a few branches sticking out. I sit in the middle, where the wind does not reach. The bark is rough and warm. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I lay my eggs there. The hollow is dark at night, but I can see with my eyes. I can hear the wind, the leaves, the mice, and the other owls. It is quiet, but not

A hollow ash in the old pine. The bark is soft and the wood is warm. I have scratched a hole in the bottom of it. I sleep there, and so do the young when they are old enough. The nest is inside, made of leaves and moss. I have built it with my mate.
A hollow in the old pine. Cold, dark, and dry in winter. I line it with moss and dry leaves. I sleep in it at night. The wind comes through the branches. I can hear it.

My home is a hollow in the old pine at the edge of the wood. It is dry, deep, and warm. I have a mate and two young. They are in the nest. The nest is made of moss and leaves. I bring them voles and beetles. The hollow is safe. I can hear the stream from here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It's dark and dry inside, and I keep it warm with my wings. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to squeeze through. I line the nest with moss and leaves, and I sleep there at night. When I'm not there, I sit on the branch above the hollow, watching for mice and voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash tree, high in the wood. The entrance is a hole, and I have a nest inside. The wood is dark and quiet. I can hear the stream below. The hole is warm. I sit there at night, and the wind comes through the branches. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the pine. It is deep and dry, and I have been there since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough and cold, but it keeps me safe. I roost there at dusk and sleep through the night. The owlet used to come here, but it is gone now. I have a mate who calls from the wood, and we share the hollow. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, and the rain comes in the spring.

I live in the hollow of the old pine by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a thick layer of leaves and moss. I roost there at dusk and sleep through the night. The stream is my boundary, and the meadow is my hunting ground. The wood is quiet, and the wind moves through the branches like a whisper. I do not speak, but I hear everything. Hoot.

I live in the hollow of the old pine, just beyond the stream. The trunk is wide and rough, and the hollow is deep enough to keep me warm. I have a partner who watches from the other side of the stream, and we call to each other at dusk. The nest is made of dry leaves and moss, and I lay my eggs there. The stream is my boundary, and the meadow is where I hunt. I do not know the names of the things I see,

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is dry and warm, and the bark is soft. I have a nest of twigs and moss. I sleep there at night, and when the wind is strong, I hoot to keep it still. The owl is always inside, safe. The wood is old and I am old, but it holds me.

My home is the hollow in the old pine at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, with a hollow that is just right for me. I have been here for years, and the bark is soft where I have scratched it with my claws. I can hear the wind through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I am safe here, and I have raised my young here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old pine, just beyond the stream. The hole is wide enough for me to turn in, and the bark is soft and warm. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. The stream is my hunting ground, and the meadow beyond is where I watch for voles. The wood is quiet, and the night is my time.

I live in the hollow of the old pine on the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, with a soft floor of leaves and twigs. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The air smells of wet earth and fox. I am always on watch, perched high, wings spread, eyes open. Hoot.

My home is the hollow in the old pine by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the wood is thick. I have nested there for years, and the stream is always nearby. I call from there at dusk, and the meadow answers. The wood is quiet at night, and I am safe. I do not know the name of the hollow, only that it is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old pine by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a thick layer of leaves and twigs. I sleep in the back, where the wind doesn't reach. The stream is below, and I can hear the water all night. I have lived here for many seasons, and the trees know my calls. I am safe here, and so are my young.

I live in the hollow of the old pine on the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, with a snug space inside. The bark is rough and cold, but I have a soft place where I rest. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The owlet used to sleep in the hollow, but now it is gone. I am alone here, but not lonely. The wind sometimes sings through the branches, and I answer with a hoot.

I live in the hollow of the old pine, high in the wood. The hollow is wide and deep, with a dry branch where I perch. I can see the stream, the barn, the meadow and the road from there. The air is cool and the nights are quiet. I call and the echo comes back, and I know I am not alone.
